en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Great Samāja,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, the Court Scattered Official and Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master of the Transmission of the Teaching, the Subject Fata, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Kapilavastu Forest together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—whose taints were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, who had attained their own benefit, whose fetters of existence were ended, and whose minds had attained mastery—numbering five thousand five hundred such persons.

At that time, there were also Śakras, Brahmās, and gods of great majesty from the ten directions, accompanied by their retinues, who, with bodies of exquisite and dignified form and radiating brilliance, came to the Kapilavastu grove. They approached the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the four Great Brahma Kings each praised the Buddha’s virtues with verses.
The first Brahma King spoke in verse:
“This Great Samaja proclaims the sound of the sublime Dharma;”
"Our Buddha is invincible; gods and humans have all gathered here.
The second Brahma King spoke in verse:
"Throughout great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he cultivated deep faith and resolve."
"Guarding the faculties such as the eye, One does not dwell amidst the realms of sensory objects.
The third Brahmā King spoke in verse:
"The reality of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom Is pure and free from defilement."
Like Śakra’s vajra, it is firm and indestructible.
The fourth Brahmā King spoke in verse:
“If a person takes refuge in the Buddha, they shall never fall into the evil realms.”
"When that person's life comes to an end, they will swiftly be reborn in the heavens.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine eye, surveyed the great assembly—the immeasurable and innumerable multitudes of humans and devas—and addressed the community of bhikṣus, saying:
"In the past, when the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas gathered assemblies of humans and devas to preach the Dharma for them, it was also just like this."
Today, I have gathered all beings of the human and celestial realms and wish to preach the Dharma for them.

You should receive and uphold it: if a person is courageous and resolute, fearless as a lion, possessing deep and firm faith that is free from attachment, then from the great earth and its mountains to the Brahma world, they shall all attain Nirvana.

When this Dharma was being taught, there were another one thousand seven hundred *śaikṣa* devas and humans, along with countless other devas, who arrived at the place where the Buddha was, illuminating everything with their radiance.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively! I observe that these assembled hosts of devas who have come here should be delivered by means of the Dharma favored by the śrāvakas.”

At that time, there were also seven thousand great yakṣas, endowed with great supernormal powers and majesty, their radiance shining brightly; accompanied by their retinues and respectfully surrounding them, they came to the Kapilavastu forest.

Furthermore, six thousand great yakṣas, dwelling upon the Golden Mountain, endowed with great supernormal powers and majestic virtue, their radiance shining brightly, came to the Kapilavastu forest together with their retinues, respectfully surrounding him.

Furthermore, three thousand great yakṣas dwelling on Mount Sātā, endowed with great supernormal powers and majesty, their radiance shining brightly, came to the Kapilavastu forest accompanied by their retinues, respectfully surrounding him.

Furthermore, there were a hundred thousand yakṣas, such as Pūrṇavīra and others, who dwelt on Mount Vaibhrāja near the city of Rājagṛha; possessing great supernormal powers and majestic virtue, their radiance shining brightly, they came to the Kapilavastu grove together with their retinues, respectfully surrounding him.

Furthermore, there were the yakṣa generals Śvāmītra, Pañcaśikha, Viśvāmitra, and others, who possessed great supernormal powers and majesty, and whose radiance shone brilliantly; together with their retinues, they came to the Kapilavastu forest.

Furthermore, there was the World-Protecting Heavenly King of the East and Lord of the Gandharvas, named Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possessed great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty; his physical form was exquisite and his radiance blazing. Surrounded by his retinue in respectful attendance, he came to the Kapilavastu forest to join the assembly and listen to the Dharma.

Also present was the World-Protecting Heavenly King of the South and Lord of the Kumbhāṇḍas, named Virūḍhaka, who possessed great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty; his physical form was exquisite and his radiance blazing. Surrounded by his retinue in respectful attendance, he came to the Kapilavastu forest to join the assembly and listen to the Dharma.

The World-Protecting Heavenly King of the western quarter, the great lord of nāgas named Virūpākṣa, possessing great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty, with a most excellent complexion and blazing radiance, came to the Kapilavastu grove together with his retinue, respectfully surrounding him, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

The World-Protecting Heavenly King of the northern quarter, the great lord of yakṣas named Kubera, possessing great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty, with a most excellent complexion and blazing radiance, came to the Kapilavastu grove together with his retinue, respectfully surrounding him, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were the attendant spirits of the Four Great Heavenly Kings—namely Maya, Kāṭi, Vikiṭi, Balyu, and Balyukṣi—who all possessed supernatural powers and influence, yet were characterized by pride and ignorance. With coarse and fierce appearances, they manifested various transformations and, surrounded by their retinues in reverent attendance, came to the Kapilavastu grove to assemble and listen to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are yakṣa generals, namely: Indrā, Mucilinda, Prajāpati,
Varuṇa, Īśāna, Candra, Kāma, Siṃhaka, Kuñjara, Nijjaṅgha, Maṇiman, and Amaṇiman.
Nīla, Praṇata, Upapañcaka, Satagiri, Sāgaravatabhūranakhendra-kumbhīḍa-yakṣa,
Aṭavakunārarāja-ji, Naliśabha-jitrasena, Khaṇḍa...
Ḍālavas, Nīlakaśatimantaras, Pañcālakhyaṇasumana-miḷikus,
together with their retinues, Ṭariphalis, Ṭarkkaṇṭhakas,
and even the worldly practitioners— all possessing supernatural powers and majestic virtue, radiating brilliant light.
Reverently surrounding him, they came to the Kapilavastu grove to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were great venomous nāgas—namely Takṣaka, Kalmāṣapāda, Pahlava, Prajāgara, Śaṅkhaśvasana, Kulika, Airāvata, and Ālāvana—who were wrathful and violent, yet possessed great supernormal powers and majesty with blazing radiance. Together with their retinues, they reverently surrounded him and came to the Kapilavastu grove to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there was a garuḍa named Abhaya, who, together with his fellow birds such as Viśuddhanetra and his retinue—all endowed with supernatural powers and majesty, their radiance shining brightly—came to the Kapilavastu forest, surrounding him with reverent devotion, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there was the invincible Vajrapāṇi, who dwells within the ocean; all the yakṣas who cause universal terror, together with their retinues—possessing supernatural powers and majestic virtue, radiating brilliant light—they came to the Kapilavastu grove, surrounding him with reverence, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there was a host of asuras—namely Vemacitra, Sucitra, Prahāda, Namuci, and one hundred sons of the Māra-asuras—together with their retinues. Possessing great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty, and radiating brilliant light, they came to the Kapilavastu grove, surrounding him with reverent devotion, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, along with their hosts of celestial beings—all endowed with supernatural powers and majestic virtue, radiating brilliant light as they respectfully surrounded him—coming to the Kapilavastu grove to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were renowned devas, namely Varuṇa-deva, Varuṇī-devī, Soma-deva, Piṣṭā-deva, Agni-deva, Mitrāvaruṇī-devī, Earth-deva, Water-deva, Fire-deva, and Wind-deva. These ten devas, possessing great majesty and virtue, manifesting through supernatural powers, together with their retinues, came to the Kapilavastu grove, shining with radiance and surrounding [the Buddha] in reverent assembly to listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were the god Nārāyaṇa, the god Saharīkṣa, the Sun God, the Moon God, the Constellation Gods, Śakra Devendra, the Maga God, and all the most venerable and holy gods, together with their two classes of attendant deities. These ten gods, possessing great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty, radiating brilliant light, came to the Kapilavastu forest, surrounding [the Buddha] with reverent devotion, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were various goddesses, namely the goddesses Sahikā, Jvālāmukhī, Ariṣṭā, Sumatī, Udamatī, Puṣpavāsini, Carcikā, Subhadra, Kacchāṅgudā, Praṇayamānā, and Śaṅkha; these and countless other goddesses, together with their retinues, possessed great supernormal powers and immeasurable majesty. With their physical forms upright and dignified, and their bodies radiating brilliant light, they respectfully surrounded him and came to the Kapilavastu forest to assemble and listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were great yakṣiṇīs, namely: the yakṣiṇī Śamā, the yakṣiṇī Mahāśamā, the yakṣiṇī Manuṣā, the yakṣiṇī Manuṣottamā, the yakṣiṇī Kṛṣṇā, the yakṣiṇī Pramukhā, the yakṣiṇī Manapramukhaka, the yakṣiṇī Marahā, the yakṣiṇī Mahāmarā, and the yakṣiṇī Bhikṣumunikā. These ten great yakṣiṇīs, likewise endowed with supernatural powers and majestic virtue, their radiance shining brightly, came to the Kapilavastu grove surrounded by their retinues in respectful attendance, having assembled to listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were ten great yakṣiṇīs, namely: the yakṣiṇī Śukrā, the yakṣiṇī Kaṇamerā, the yakṣiṇī Karuṇā, the yakṣiṇī Nīlakāvasinī, the yakṣiṇī Avantakīśā, the yakṣiṇī Pramukhibhedakāvasinī, the yakṣiṇī Sanmatā, the yakṣiṇī Haritī, and the yakṣiṇī Rucikā. These yakṣiṇīs, likewise endowed with supernatural powers and majestic virtue, their radiance shining brightly, came to the Kapilavastu grove accompanied by their retinues, respectfully surrounding him as they gathered to listen to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there were also the Hārītī and her retinue of boys and girls, who likewise possessed majestic power and supernormal faculties; with their radiance shining brightly, they came to the Kapilavastu grove, surrounded by their attendants in reverent circumambulation, to assemble and listen to the Dharma.
In this manner, the Brahma kings, Śakras, devas and humans, the eight classes of supernatural beings, and the great bhikṣus—immeasurable and innumerable—all gathered together.
At that time, within the assembly there was a Great Black Spirit named Jūḍana, who possessed great supernormal powers.

Fierce and violent, he tormented humans and devas and obstructed their cultivation of wholesome deeds. Striking the ground with his hand, he let out a great, evil cry; from the midst of the void, he conjured various malevolent signs such as great winds, clouds, lightning, hail, and thunderbolts, causing all the assembly to be struck with terror.
The Buddha immediately observed him and uttered the sound:
"Hear the Dharma.
Having heard it, Māra took refuge and ceased his evil ways; he then dwelt together with the bhikṣus in the Śrāvaka-yāna.
At that time, the assembly, seeing the Buddha subdue Māra, leaped for joy and, with faith and acceptance, practiced accordingly.
This is the *Buddha-bhāṣita-mahāsāmājika-sūtra*.
